0158               
0159               ; While we don't mean to USE the console ROM, for interrupts we
0160               ; are forced to interface with some of it. We need these addresses
0161               ; to minimize what it does so we can maximize our use of scratchpad.
0162               ; While I'd like to use the cassette hook - requires only 10 instructions
0163               ; and only uses 6 words of scratchpad, we can't here because it
0164               ; loses the return address, meaning you can only use it if you
0165               ; know where your LIMI 2 is and interrupts are otherwise disabled. So
0166               ; we have to use the longer but more standard interrupt hook, which also
0167               ; reads VDP status for us (no choice).
0168               
0169      8379     intcnt              equ >8379   ; interrupt counter byte, adds 1 (from GPLWS r14) every frame
0170      837B     vdp_status          equ >837B   ; VDP status byte mirror
0171      83C2     intwsr1             equ >83c2   ; INT WS R1  - interrupt control flags - must be >8000
0172      83C4     intwsr2             equ >83c4   ; INT WS R2  - address of user interrupt routine (point to int_handler)
0173      83D6     intwsr11            equ >83d6   ; screen timeout counter - must be odd (init to 1, is inct every frame)
0174      83DA     intwsr13            equ >83da   ; INT WS R13 - used for interrupt call (word)
0175      83DC     intwsr14            equ >83dc   ; INT WS R14 - used for interrupt call (word)
0176      83DE     intwsr15            equ >83de   ; INT WS R15 - used for interrupt call (word)
0177      83F6     gplwsr11            equ >83f6   ; GPL WS R11 - return address to interrupt ROM (not used, but overwritten each int)
0178      83F8     gplwsr12            equ >83f8   ; GPL WS R12 - used for cassette test and interrupt hook test (zeroed each int)
0179      83FA     gplwsr13            equ >83fa   ; GPL WS R13 - used in my interrupt handler
0180      83FC     gplwsr14            equ >83fc   ; GPL WS R14 - flags used to detect cassette - must be >0108 (or at least >0020 clear)
0181      83FE     gplwsr15            equ >83fe   ; GPL WS R15 - base address of VDP for status read - must be >8C02

0470               ; Load sprite definitions: Sprite number in R4, CPU data in R0, count of sprites in R5 (MSB)
0471               ; Original: pointer = sprite number, temp = CPU address, a = number sprites
0472               ; Note: sprites are all expected to be double-size 16x16, 32 bytes each, so sprite char 1 is character 4
0473               ; Sprite pattern table at >3800
0474               define_sprite
0475 A1DA C20B  18     mov r11,r8          ; save return
0476 A1DC C080  18     mov r0,r2           ; Source data.
0477 A1DE C004  18     mov r4,r0           ; VRAM target.
0478 A1E0 0A50  26     sla r0,5            ; sprite number times 32 for bytes
0479 A1E2 0220  22     ai r0,>3800         ; add VDP base
     A1E4 3800     
0480 A1E6 C0C5  18     mov r5,r3		; Length.
0481 A1E8 0983  32     srl r3,8            ; make int
0482 A1EA 0A53  26     sla r3,5            ; count times 32
0483 A1EC 0300  22     limi 0              ; ints off
     A1EE 0000     
0484 A1F0 06A0  32     bl @LDIRVM          ; do the copy
     A1F2 A076     
0485 A1F4 0300  22     limi 2              ; ints on
     A1F6 0002     
0486 A1F8 0458  20     b *r8               ; back to caller
0487               
0488               ; Load character definitions: Char number in R1, CPU data in R2, count in R3 (MSB)
0489               ; Original: pointer = char number, temp = CPU address, a = number chars
0490               ; Note this loads the pattern three times if in bitmap mode (MODE&0x04)
0491               ; Pattern table at >0000
0492               define_char
0493 A1FA C20B  18     mov r11,r8          ; save return
0494 A1FC C080  18     mov r0,r2           ; source data
0495 A1FE C004  18     mov r4,r0           ; move input to scratch
0496 A200 0A30  22     sla r0,3            ; char number times 8 (VDP base is 0, so already there)
0497 A202 C0C5  18     mov r5,r3
0498 A204 0983  32     srl r3,8            ; make word
0499 A206 0A33  22     sla r3,3            ; count times 8
0500 A208 D160  30     movb @mode,r5       ; get mode flags
     A20A 834E     
0501 A20C 0245  22     andi r5,>0800
     A20E 0800     
0502 A210 1607  14     jne !1              ; not in bitmap mode, do a single copy
0503               
0504 A212 0300  22     limi 0              ; ints off
     A214 0000     
0505 A216 06A0  32     bl @LDIRVM3         ; do the triple copy
     A218 A090     
0506 A21A 0300  22     limi 2              ; ints on
     A21C 0002     
0507 A21E 0458  20     b *r8               ; back to caller
0508               
0509               !1
0510 A220 0300  22     limi 0              ; ints off
     A222 0000     
0511 A224 06A0  32     bl @LDIRVM          ; do the single copy
     A226 A076     
0512 A228 0300  22     limi 2              ; ints on
     A22A 0002     
0513 A22C 0458  20     b *r8               ; back to caller
0514               
0515               ; Load bitmap color definitions: Char number in R1, CPU data in R2, count in R3 (MSB)
0516               ; Original: pointer = char number, temp = CPU address, a = number chars
0517               ; Note: always does the triple copy. Color table at >2000
0518               define_color
0519 A22E C20B  18     mov r11,r8          ; save return
0520 A230 C080  18     mov r0,r2           ; source data
0521 A232 C004  18     mov r4,r0           ; move input to scratch
0522 A234 0A30  22     sla r0,3            ; char number times 8
0523 A236 0220  22     ai r0,>2000         ; add base address
     A238 2000     
0524 A23A C0C5  18     mov r5,r3
0525 A23C 0983  32     srl r3,8            ; make word
0526 A23E 0A33  22     sla r3,3            ; count times 8
0527 A240 0300  22     limi 0              ; ints off
     A242 0000     
0528 A244 06A0  32     bl @LDIRVM3         ; do the triple copy
     A246 A090     
0529 A248 0300  22     limi 2              ; ints on
     A24A 0002     
0530 A24C 0458  20     b *r8               ; back to caller
0531               
0532               ; Update sprite entry - copy data (4 bytes) to sprite table mirror at sprites
0533               ; R4 = sprite number, R5 = byte 1, r6 = byte 2, r7 = byte 3, r0 = byte 4 (all MSB)
0534               ; Original: A = sprite number, source data at sprite_data
0535               update_sprite
0536 A24E 0984  32     srl r4,8            ; make word
0537 A250 0A24  20     sla r4,2            ; x4 for address
0538 A252 0224  22     ai r4,sprites       ; sprite mirror address
     A254 2000     
0539 A256 DD05  32     movb r5,*r4+        ; move bytes
0540 A258 DD06  32     movb r6,*r4+        ; move bytes
0541 A25A DD07  32     movb r7,*r4+        ; move bytes
0542 A25C DD00  32     movb r0,*r4+        ; move bytes
0543 A25E 045B  20     b *r11
0544               
0545               ; SGN R0 - return 1, -1 or 0 as 16 bit
0546               _sgn16
0547 A260 C000  18     mov r0,r0       ; check for zero
0548 A262 1306  14     jeq !1          ; if yes, we're done
0549 A264 0240  22     andi r0,>8000   ; check for negative
     A266 8000     
0550 A268 1302  14     jeq !2          ; was not
0551 A26A 0700  14     seto r0         ; was negative, make it -1
0552 A26C 045B  20     b *r11          ; back to caller
0553               !2
0554 A26E 0580  14     inc r0          ; we know it was zero, and we want 1
0555               !1
0556 A270 045B  20     b *r11          ; back to caller
0557               
0558               ; 16-bit signed modulo. R1 % R2 = R0 - 9900 doesn't do signed divide
0559               ; original was stack%stack=YYAA
0560               ; Remainder is negative if the dividend was negative
0561               _mod16s
0562 A272 04C0  14     clr r0          ; make dividend 32-bit
0563 A274 C082  18     mov r2,r2       ; check divisor for zero
0564 A276 130A  14     jeq !1
0565 A278 0742  18     abs r2          ; make sure divisor is positive
0566 A27A C041  18     mov r1,r1       ; check sign of dividend
0567 A27C 1505  14     jgt !2          ; go do the faster positive version
0568               
0569 A27E 0741  18     abs r1          ; was negative, make it positive
0570 A280 3C02 128     div r2,r0       ; do the division => r2=quotient, r3=remainder
0571 A282 0501  14     neg r1          ; make remainder negative
0572 A284 C001  18     mov r1,r0       ; into r0
0573 A286 045B  20     b *r11
0574               
0575               !2
0576 A288 3C02 128     div r2,r0       ; do the division => r2=quotient, r3=remainder
0577 A28A C001  18     mov r1,r0       ; into r0
0578               !1
0579 A28C 045B  20     b *r11
0580               
0581               ; 16-bit signed divide. R1 / R2 = R0 - 9900 doesn't do signed divide
0582               ; original was stack/stack=YYAA
0583               ; Remainder is negative if the signs differ
0584               _div16s
0585 A28E 04C0  14     clr r0          ; make dividend 32-bit
0586 A290 C0C2  18     mov r2,r3       ; check divisor for zero
0587 A292 1308  14     jeq !1          ;
0588 A294 28C1  18     xor r1,r3
0589 A296 0742  18     abs r2
0590 A298 0741  18     abs r1          ; might as well make them positive now that we have copies
0591 A29A 3C02 128     div r2,r0       ; do the divide => r0=quotient, r1=remainder
0592 A29C 0243  22     andi r3,>8000   ; mask out sign bit
     A29E 8000     
0593 A2A0 1301  14     jeq !1          ; skip ahead to positive version
0594               
0595 A2A2 0500  14     neg r0          ; negate the result
0596               !1
0597 A2A4 045B  20     b *r11
0598               
0599               ; Random number generator - return in R0, (complex one uses R3,R4, simpler one only R0)
0600               ; Original output into YYAA
0601               random
0628               ; simpler one from dreamcast days...

     A2A8 834C

0631 A2AC 1702  14     jnc .rand1          ; jump if no 1

     A2B0 A2B8     
0633               .rand1
0634 A2B2 C800  30     mov r0,@lfsr        ; save the output
     A2B4 834C     
0635 A2B6 045B  20     b *r11
0636               rmask
0637 A2B8 B400         data >b400          ; mask for 16 bit
0639               
0640               ; Set SN Frequency: R0=frequency code, R2=channel command (MSB)
0641               ; Original: A=least significant byte  X=channel command  Y=most significant byte
0642               sn76489_freq
0643 A2BA C0C0  18     mov r0,r3

     A2BE 000F

     A2C6 8400

0649 A2CA 0240  22     andi r0,>003f
     A2CC 003F

0651 A2D0 D800  30     movb r0,@SOUND  ; most significant byte
     A2D2 8400     
0652 A2D4 045B  20     b *r11
0653               
0654               ; Set SN volume: R0=volume (MSB, inverse of attenuation), R2=channel command (MSB)

0656               sn76489_vol

     A2E0 8400

0832               
0833               ; this is where interrupts happen every frame
0834               ; Unlike a normal TI application, this one runs with interrupts ON,
0835               ; so all operations need to be sure to protect VDP address with LIMI 0,
0836               ; as well as any operations that might need to manipulate data managed
0837               ; by this interrupt. We enter via the normal user hook, so WP is on
0838               ; GPLWS, interrupts are off, and the VDP is already reset and status
0839               ; stashed on vdp_status (>837b). Our return address to the ROM is in
0840               ; r11, but we are NOT going to use it so that we don't need to reserve
0841               ; r8 for whatever nonsense it does. That means we need to load intws
0842               ; and RTWP ourselves at the end. We are on our own workspace so we
0843               ; don't have to worry about the main app's workspace.
0844               int_handler
0845               ; first copy the sprite table
0846 A48E 02E0  18     lwpi myintwp        ; separate safe workspace
     A490 8320     
0847               
0849 A492 C820  46     mov @>7ffe,@saved_bank  ; save bank switch page
     A494 7FFE     
     A496 8352     
0851               
0852 A498 020B  20     li r11,>005b        ; >1b00 with the write bit added, and byte flipped
     A49A 005B     
0853 A49C D80B  30     movb r11,@VDPWADR   ; SAL address
     A49E 8C02     
0854 A4A0 06CB  14     swpb r11
0855 A4A2 D80B  30     movb r11,@VDPWADR   ; going to copy the sprite table to VDP
     A4A4 8C02     
0856               
0857 A4A6 D2E0  30     movb @mode,r11
     A4A8 834E     
0858 A4AA 024B  22     andi r11,>0400      ; if bit >04 (inhibit flicker) is cleared, jump ahead to rotate
     A4AC 0400     
0859 A4AE 130A  14     jeq !4
0860               
0861 A4B0 04CB  14     clr r11             ; else we're going to just write it straight across
0862 A4B2 020C  20     li r12,128
     A4B4 0080     
0863 A4B6 020D  20     li r13,sprites
     A4B8 2000     
0864               !7
0865 A4BA D83D  40     movb *r13+,@VDPWDATA
     A4BC 8C00     
0866 A4BE 060C  14     dec r12
0867 A4C0 16FC  14     jne -!7
0868 A4C2 101B  14     jmp !5
0869               
0870               !4
0871 A4C4 D2E0  30     movb @flicker,r11   ; here we write it rotated every frame
     A4C6 834F     
0872 A4C8 022B  22     ai r11,>0400
     A4CA 0400     
0873 A4CC 024B  22     andi r11,>7f00
     A4CE 7F00     
0874 A4D0 D80B  30     movb r11,@flicker
     A4D2 834F     
0875 A4D4 06CB  14     swpb r11            ; make count
0876 A4D6 020C  20     li r12,32           ; count
     A4D8 0020     
0877               
0878               !6
0879 A4DA 022B  22     ai r11,sprites        ; this is still faster than separate incs
     A4DC 2000

0890               ; next read the joysticks - output needs to be 21xxLDRU - 1 and 2 are button and button2 respectively
0891               ; We don't have a button 2. We also need to read the keyboard and fill in key1_data. key2_data we
0892               ; will leave unused. Note key1_data expects Coleco-style 0-9,10-*,11-#,15=not pressed, but we can throw
0893               ; everything else as ASCII. We could do a split keyboard for 2 players, but I guess we'll leave it for now.

     A522 0006

1018               ; given a joystick read in r13, return bits in r12

1929               ; The stack is simulated using R10. It's not used in
1930               ; these functions but the compiled code will need it.
1931               ; To push: dect r10, mov r0,*r10
1932               ; To pop:  mov *r10+,r0
1933               ; However, for JSR a function is helpful - call this like:
1934               ; bl @jsr
1935               ; data <function_address>
1936               jsr
1937 A980 C3BB  30     mov *r11+,r14       ; get the jump address
1938 A982 064A  14     dect r10            ; make room on stack
1939 A984 C68B  30     mov r11,*r10        ; save return address
1940 A986 069E  24     bl *r14             ; new subroutine call, we can come back here
1941 A988 C2FA  30     mov *r10+,r11       ; get real return off stack - warning, all basic functions do this inline rather than return
1942 A98A 045B  20     b *r11              ; back to caller

1984               ;;; CVBasic code starts here
1985               	; 	' ==========================================================================
1986               	; 	' KEYSTONE KAPERS -- CVBasic, dual target TI-99/4A + ColecoVision.
1987               	; 	'
1988               	; 	' Garry Kitchen's 1983 Activision game. See DESIGN.md; 0 records the
1989               	; 	' research and the four places the sources disagree.
1990               	; 	'
1991               	; 	' Fifty seconds to run Harry Hooligan down inside a department store eight
1992               	; 	' screens wide and four levels tall, before he reaches the roof.
1993               	; 	'
1994               	; 	' THE THREE DECISIONS THIS FILE IS BUILT ON, all from DESIGN.md:
1995               	; 	'
1996               	; 	'   * THE VIEW FLIPS, IT DOES NOT SCROLL. Eight discrete screens; crossing
1997               	; 	'     an edge blits the next one. The per-frame budget never pays for the
1998               	; 	'     store at all -- RallyX repaints 576 chars every camera cell and had
1999               	; 	'     to have all its movement rewritten to survive that.
2000               	; 	'   * A SCREEN IS EXACTLY 256 PX, so an actor's x within its screen is one
2001               	; 	'     unsigned byte. No 16-bit world coordinate exists in this program.
2002               	; 	'   * ZERO PER-FRAME VDP READS. An actor's floor is an index into flry(),
2003               	; 	'     never a question asked of the screen, so the Ms. Pac-Man trap
2004               	; 	'     (actors x per-actor search) is absent by construction.
2005               	; 	'
2006               	; 	' The rules that shaped the code, all from CLAUDE.md 3A, because every one
2007               	; 	' of them fails SILENTLY:
2008               	; 	'
2009               	; 	'   * A plain variable is 8-BIT and a CONST over 255 TRUNCATES. Every
2010               	; 	'     name-table offset past row 7 is a #var or a bare literal.
2011               	; 	'   * Every #var comparison is UNSIGNED.
2012               	; 	'   * `<cmp> AND <cmp>` is miscompiled by the 9900 backend. Nested IFs.
2013               	; 	'   * A sprite at y=208 TERMINATES the sprite list. Hidden sprites go 209.
2014               	; 	'   * A GOSUB left by GOTO never pops. Death, catch and escape are STATES
2015               	; 	'     set in a routine and acted on at the top of the main loop.
2016               	; 	'   * MPY clobbers r0. Nothing here multiplies into an index -- the tables
2017               	; 	'     tsrc()/bdst()/lv8() exist precisely so that no multiply is needed on
2018               	; 	'     a path that reads the result back.
2019               	; 	' ==========================================================================
2020               	;
2021               	; 	' ---------------------------------------------------------------- BANKING
2022               	; 	' THE ART AND THE STORE MAP LIVE IN ROM BANK 1 ON THE TI. The fixed area
2023               	; 	' is 24,336 bytes -- three 8,112-byte loader pages -- and unbanked this
2024               	; 	' program filled 24,304 of them, so there was no room left for anything at
2025               	; 	' all. `linkticart` does not warn when you exceed it; it silently discards
2026               	; 	' the top of the image, and what goes missing is whatever sits nearest the
2027               	; 	' end, usually a DATA block rather than code. Nothing errors.
2028               	; 	'
2029               	; 	' WHAT IS SAFE TO BANK. Everything moved here is read at SETUP (the
2030               	; 	' DEFINE CHAR / DEFINE SPRITE calls) or on a screen crossing (the template
2031               	; 	' blit and the escalator's phase tables) -- and, because there is exactly
2032               	; 	' ONE data bank and it is selected ONCE at startup and never switched, it
2033               	; 	' stays mapped for the life of the program. The rule in CLAUDE.md 3A is
2034               	; 	' about SWITCHING inside a frame or under the vblank ISR; with a single
2035               	; 	' permanently-selected bank there is no switch to miss. A missed
2036               	; 	' BANK SELECT would return bytes from the wrong page with no error at
2037               	; 	' build or run time, which is why there is only one and it is set before
2038               	; 	' anything reads from it.
2039               	; 	'
2040               	; 	' BANK ROM 128 sizes ColecoVision's Megacart mapper, NOT the TI cart --
2041               	; 	' that comes from how many bank files the assembler emits -- and it is
2042               	; 	' one of only four values the compiler accepts (128/256/512/1024).
2043               	; 	' The whole thing is gated on TI994A: the Coleco build is Z80 and roughly
2044               	; 	' half the size, so it neither needs banking nor wants to become a
2045               	; 	' Megacart image.
2046               	; 	#if TI994A
2047               	; 	BANK ROM 128
2048               	; 	#endif
2049               	; 	CONST SPRHID = 209		' NOT 208 -- 208 terminates the sprite list
2050      00D1     const_SPRHID	equ >00d1
2051               	;
2052               	; 	' ------------------------------------------------------------- geometry
2053               	; 	' A band is 5 rows: 4 rows of air (32 px) over one floor slab. Standing
2054               	; 	' Kelly is 16 px, so headroom is 16 px and the jump apex is 14 -- two
2055               	; 	' short of the ceiling, because an arc that bonks is silently truncated.
2056               	; 	' 4 px/frame = 240 px/s. At 2 it was not merely sluggish, it was
2057               	; 	' ARITHMETICALLY TOO SLOW: the climb is three traverses = 6,144 px, which
2058               	; 	' at 2 px/frame is 51 seconds of pure running against a 50-second clock,
2059               	; 	' before a single obstacle, escalator ride or catch. At 3 it is 34 s --
2060               	; 	' and 34 s was still wrong, for a reason a per-actor speed check cannot
2061               	; 	' see: HARRY'S CLIMB IS ALSO 34 s (DESIGN.md 4a). Kelly being 1.5x faster
2062               	; 	' bought nothing, because Harry's route is two thirds the length of
2063               	; 	' Kelly's -- he spawns beside floor 2's escalator and effectively skips a
2064               	; 	' traverse. A chase resolves on PATH / SPEED, not on speed, and the two
2065               	; 	' quotients were equal, so pursuit on foot could never close. At 4 the
2066               	; 	' climb is 25 s against Harry's 45, and the elevator buys back more.
2067               	; 	CONST WALKSP = 4		' px per PASS -- the old unit, kept only for
2068      0004     const_WALKSP	equ >0004
2069               	; 					' the checkers' arithmetic and the comments
2070               	; 					' that quote it. Nothing moves by it now.
2071               	; 	' SIXTY-FOURTHS OF A PIXEL PER FRAME, which is what he actually walks by.
2072               	; 	'
2073               	; 	' HIS OLD BEST-CASE SPEED, MADE CONSTANT -- not his old average. WALKSP was
2074               	; 	' 4 px per loop PASS, so what he actually did depended on the screen: 104 px/s
2075               	; 	' on a light one at 26 passes/s, 80 px/s on the lift and escalator screens at
2076               	; 	' 20. Matching the MEASURED AVERAGE of 23.8 passes/s gave 95.6 px/s (102/64),
2077               	; 	' which is the same average and an 8% loss on exactly the screens a chase
2078               	; 	' spends most of its time crossing -- the crook was already per-frame and did
2079               	; 	' not change, so the ratio that decides the chase quietly dropped. Played, it
2080               	; 	' read as only just catching him on the last screen.
2081               	; 	'
2082               	; 	' 111/64 is 104.1 px/s: his best case, everywhere. He is now at least as fast
2083               	; 	' as he ever was on any screen rather than faster on some and slower on
2084               	; 	' others, and the chase margin goes from 10.6 s to 17.3 s.
2085               	; 	CONST KWALK64 = 111
2086      006F     const_KWALK64	equ >006f
2087               	; 	' The bounce phase, in sixty-fourths of a phase per frame. 32 phases at
2088               	; 	' 25/64 per frame is 1.37 s an arc, against the 1.35 s one phase per pass
2089               	; 	' gives at 23.8 passes a second.
2090               	; 	CONST BOUNCE64 = 25
2091      0019     const_BOUNCE64	equ >0019
2092               	; 	CONST XWALL = 232		' furthest left edge at the store's east wall
2093      00E8     const_XWALL	equ >00e8
2094               	; 	CONST XWALW = 8			' nearest left edge at the west wall
2095      0008     const_XWALW	equ >0008
2096               	; 	CONST STANDH = 24		' Kelly standing -- TWO SPRITES tall
2097      0018     const_STANDH	equ >0018
2098               	; 	' KELLY DUCKED. It was 8 px, which is not a crouch -- it is a squash, with
2099               	; 	' no room to draw a figure bending in a DIRECTION. 11 px is, and the
2100               	; 	' biplane is raised to match (obh below, and the hitbox in coll_obst):
2101               	; 	' with the plane at 16..22 an 11 px crouch passes five pixels under it and
2102               	; 	' a 24 px standing Kop does not. The apex is 14, so a jump still cannot
2103               	; 	' clear it either -- the plane stays the one obstacle that must be ducked.
2104               	; 	'
2105               	; 	' AND 11 IS THE CEILING, not a preference. Duckable means the obstacle
2106               	; 	' clears the crouch, jumpable means it clears under the apex; raising the
2107               	; 	' crouch raises the duckable floor, so past 11 a band of beach-ball
2108               	; 	' heights is neither. A sweep of every crouch height against every ball
2109               	; 	' hitbox puts the limit at 11, and shrinking the ball does not move it --
2110               	; 	' the apex is what binds. assets/checkball.py fails the build on it.
2111               	; 	CONST DUCKH = 11		' Kelly ducked -- bent over, not squashed
2112      000B     const_DUCKH	equ >000b
2113               	; 	CONST CATCHR = 12
2114      000C     const_CATCHR	equ >000c
2115               	; 	' HOW CLOSE VERTICALLY A CATCH NEEDS. A floor is a whole storey apart, so
2116               	; 	' anything under a character row means they are genuinely level; a rider
2117               	; 	' eight pixels up a flight is already clear of a Kop standing beside it.
2118               	; 	CONST CATCHV = 8		' catch / hit radius, centre to centre
2119      0008     const_CATCHV	equ >0008
2120               	;
2121               	; 	' Kelly states
2122               	; 	CONST ST_RUN = 0
2123      0000     const_ST_RUN	equ >0000
2124               	; 	CONST ST_JUMP = 1
2125      0001     const_ST_JUMP	equ >0001
2126               	; 	CONST ST_DUCK = 2
2127      0002     const_ST_DUCK	equ >0002
2128               	; 	CONST ST_ESC = 3		' riding an escalator -- no input, invincible
2129      0003     const_ST_ESC	equ >0003
2130               	; 	CONST ST_ELEV = 4		' inside the car     -- no input, invincible
2131      0004     const_ST_ELEV	equ >0004
2132               	;
2133               	; 	' obstacle kinds, matching assets/genstore.py
2134               	; 	CONST OB_CART = 1
2135      0001     const_OB_CART	equ >0001
2136               	; 	CONST OB_BALL = 2
2137      0002     const_OB_BALL	equ >0002
2138               	; 	CONST OB_RADIO = 3
2139      0003     const_OB_RADIO	equ >0003
2140               	; 	CONST OB_PLANE = 4
2141      0004     const_OB_PLANE	equ >0004
2142               	;
2143               	; 	' sprite patterns (DEFINE SPRITE index n -> pattern n*4)
2144               	; 	' THE VDP CANNOT MIRROR A SPRITE -- there is no flip bit -- so every actor
2145               	; 	' that runs both ways carries a second set of frames. assets/genart.py
2146               	; 	' generates the left ones from the right ones so the two directions are
2147               	; 	' guaranteed identical.
2148               	; 	' KELLY AND HARRY ARE 24 PX -- a 16 px top sprite with the top half of a
2149               	; 	' second sprite below it. A band gives 32 px of air plus the 7 px of the
2150               	; 	' ceiling row under its 1 px slab line = 39 px, and 24 + the 14 px jump is
2151               	; 	' 38. The apex CANNOT be reduced to buy room: at 10 px the ball's jump and
2152               	; 	' duck windows stop overlapping and a dead band opens (DESIGN.md 5a).
2153               	; 	'
2154               	; 	' The two sprites never share a scanline, so a band still costs Kelly 1 +
2155               	; 	' Harry 1 + two obstacles = four per line.
2156               	; 	' Pattern numbers are genart.py's SPRITES order x 4. Move one there and
2157               	; 	' this table must move with it -- nothing checks the correspondence.
2158               	; 	' SPRITE PATTERNS, laid out by genart.py so the selection code is three
2159               	; 	' statements rather than two mirrored branches. Everything that FACES comes
2160               	; 	' in a RIGHT block and then a LEFT block of the same shape, so changing
2161               	; 	' facing is one fixed offset; the LEGS do not face and are shared.
2162               	; 	CONST P_KHAT = 0		' Kelly RIGHT: hat, black

2466               	; 	' THERE ARE ONLY TWO SAFE ANSWERS AND THE SCREEN ONLY FITS ONE OF THEM.
2467               	; 	' Kelly closes on an oncoming ball at WALKSP + 2 = 6 px a pass, so:
2468               	; 	'
2469               	; 	'   <= 54 px   ONE JUMP CLEARS BOTH -- the arc holds its 14 px apex for
2470               	; 	'              nine passes, which is 54 px of closing distance
2471               	; 	'   >= 168 px  he can LAND BETWEEN them -- the arc is airborne for 28
2472               	; 	'              passes, which is 168 px
2473               	; 	'

2475               	; 	' too close to land between. The gap shipped at 46 px west of the lift and
2476               	; 	' 70 px east of it -- 46 is inside the first window and 70 is squarely in
2477               	; 	' that middle, which is the asymmetry that got reported.
2478               	; 	'

2480               	; 	' a bigger gap moves the second hazard TOWARD the player: at 168 px it
2481               	; 	' starts within 72 px of the wall he walks in through, and at 176 it lands
2482               	; 	' essentially on top of him with no time to read it. That was tried and it
2483               	; 	' is worse than the bug it replaced.

2486               	; 	' and it leaves the nearer hazard at least 192 px away at entry. The pair

2488               	; 	' original's paired hazards read like. assets/checkspace.py checks all of
2489               	; 	' it and checkspace_test.py proves it rejects 70 and 176 alike.

2494               	; 	CONST ELOPEN = 85		' = ELWAIT - ELDOOR, as a literal: a CONST
2495      0055     const_ELOPEN	equ >0055
2496               	; 					' built from other CONSTs is exactly the
2497               	; 					' folded-constant trap in CLAUDE.md 3A
2498               	;
2499               	; 	' escalator boarding zones, in CENTRE-x pixels
2500               	; 	' ESCALATOR BOARDING ZONES, IN PIXELS, AND THEY TRACK THE ART.
2501               	; 	' The flight is drawn as four rows of two characters stepping two columns
2502               	; 	' per row: west runs cols 1-2 (top) down to 7-8 (foot), east runs 29-30
2503               	; 	' (top) down to 23-24 (foot). These zones ARE those columns x8. When the
2504               	; 	' escalator art changed from a filled triangle to a stepped flight the
2505               	; 	' foot moved, and a boarding zone left where it was would put the player
2506               	; 	' on a staircase that is not under them -- no error, just a floor that
2507               	; 	' teleports you when you walk over an empty patch of it.
2508               	; 	' THESE ARE THE DRAWN STEPS, in screen pixels. The flight is fifteen
2509               	; 	' characters wide: its foot tread sits at x 95-103 (west) and 152-160
2510               	; 	' (east), its head tread at 23-31 and 224-232. An actor rides between
2511               	; 	' those, so the numbers here are the ART's, and moving the art without
2512               	; 	' moving them puts the rider beside the escalator rather than on it.
2513               	; 	' THE RIDER STANDS ON A STEP, and everything about the ride follows from
2514               	; 	' WHICH ONE. The staircase is a straight line -- a step 4 px higher is 8
2515               	; 	' px further along it -- so one number, the step's height above the floor
2516               	; 	' being left, fixes both the rider's x and the rest of the ride:
2517               	; 	'
2518               	; 	'     west  klx = 99 - 2*height        east  klx = 140 + 2*height
2519               	; 	'
2520               	; 	' The bottom step is 4 px up, so a rider walking on boards at klx = 91
2521               	; 	' (west) or 148 (east); the head step is 40 up, so the ride ends at 19 or
2522               	; 	' 220. Those are the ART's numbers -- the foot tread is drawn at x 95-103
2523               	; 	' west and 152-160 east, the head tread at 23-31 and 224-232 -- so moving
2524               	; 	' the art without moving these puts the rider beside the staircase.
2525               	; 	'
2526               	; 	' THE PHASE MATTERS. The steps climb 1 px a frame and the animation runs
2527               	; 	' four 1 px phases, so the bottom step is 4 + escp px up, not 4. Boarding
2528               	; 	' without that term leaves the feet up to 3 px out of register with the
2529               	; 	' tread and the whole ride drifts, which is exactly what "he floats
2530               	; 	' beside the steps" looked like.
2531               	; 	CONST ESCFX = 91		' west foot: rider's x when boarding
2532      005B     const_ESCFX	equ >005b
2533               	; 	CONST ESCFXE = 148		' east foot
2534      0094     const_ESCFXE	equ >0094
2535               	; 	CONST ESCHX = 19		' west head: rider's x on arrival
2536      0013     const_ESCHX	equ >0013
2537               	; 	CONST ESCHXE = 220		' east head
2538      00DC     const_ESCHXE	equ >00dc
2539               	; 	CONST ESCRISE = 40		' floor to floor, and the ride's length
2540      0028     const_ESCRISE	equ >0028
2541               	;
2542               	; 	' TIMER UNITS PER KROOK, AND A UNIT IS NOT A SECOND. Measured off the
2543               	; 	' reference video (DESIGN.md 0m): the original counts 50 down to 0 and a
2544               	; 	' unit lasts 1.99 s, so a round is about 100 seconds. TICKFR below is
2545               	; 	' what makes it so here.
2546               	; 	CONST TIMEL = 50		' timer units per Krook
2547      0032     const_TIMEL	equ >0032
2548               	; 	' FRAMES PER TIMER UNIT. 120, not 60, and this is not cosmetic -- it is
2549               	; 	' what makes a round finishable. Everything that MOVES in this game is
2550               	; 	' paced per loop PASS, and the loop runs about 25 passes a second, so
2551               	; 	' Kelly's 4 px a pass is ~100 px/s (the reference's Kelly is 102, so the
2552               	; 	' speeds match). The timer, though, is paced by the frame DELTA -- real
2553               	; 	' wall-clock time. At 60 frames a unit the round was 50 real seconds
2554               	; 	' while Kelly's route to the roof takes about 72, so the clock ran out
2555               	; 	' before either of them could get there and every round ended on a
2556               	; 	' timeout. checkchase.py hid it by assuming 60 passes a second; it now
2557               	; 	' models the real rate.
2558               	; 	CONST TICKFR = 120
2559      0078     const_TICKFR	equ >0078
2560               	; 	' NINE TIMER UNITS -- not ten, and not nine seconds. Every source says a
2561               	; 	' cart, ball or radio costs "9 seconds", and what they mean is the number
2562               	; 	' on the HUD, because that is what the manual calls seconds. So the
2563               	; 	' DISPLAYED count drops by 9. A unit is about two real seconds
2564               	; 	' (DESIGN.md 0m), which makes one careless cart cost roughly eighteen --
2565               	; 	' close to a fifth of the round, and the reason the refractory latch
2566               	; 	' below matters so much.
2567               	; 	CONST HITPEN = 9		' timer units a cart / ball / radio costs
2568      0009     const_HITPEN	equ >0009
2569               	; 	' HOW LONG A HIT SOUNDS, IN LOOP PASSES -- and therefore how long the
2570               	; 	' store stands still for one. The two are the same number on purpose:
2571               	; 	' the freeze is meant to last exactly as long as the noise, so a change
2572               	; 	' to one that did not move the other would leave either a silent pause
2573               	; 	' or a sound playing over a resumed game. Passes, not frames, because
2574               	; 	' both counters are spent once per pass in sfx_tick and the main loop.
2575               	; 	CONST HITSND = 20
2576      0014     const_HITSND	equ >0014
2577               	; 	CONST HITREF = 45		' frames before the SAME obstacle can charge
2578      002D     const_HITREF	equ >002d
2579               	; 					' again. See coll_obst -- clearing the latch
2580               	; 					' on the first non-overlapping frame is not
2581               	; 					' enough, because a bouncing ball leaves
2582               	; 					' contact between bounces.
2583               	;
2584               	; 	' ---------------------------------------------------------------- tables
2585               	; 	DIM flry(4)			' floor surface y, by level
2586               	; 	DIM #bdst(4)			' band name-table offset, by level
2587               	; 	DIM #tsrc(15)			' template source offset, by template id
2588               	; 	DIM lv8(4)			' lv*8, so no multiply lands on an index
2589               	; 	DIM jarc(32)			' the jump arc: 30 frames, apex 14
2590               	; 	DIM msk(8)
2591               	;
2592               	; 	' EIGHT obstacle slots -- TWO per band, and that number is forced.
2593               	; 	'
2594               	; 	' The VDP shows four sprites per scanline and DROPS the rest by slot
2595               	; 	' order; it does not flicker them, they simply are not there. Three per
2596               	; 	' band was sized against Kelly alone (1 + 3 = 4) and forgot that HARRY
2597               	; 	' can be on that band too -- and when he is, the fifth sprite on his
2598               	; 	' scanline is the highest-numbered obstacle, which vanishes while still
2599               	; 	' being solid. An invisible thing that costs nine seconds is the worst
2600               	; 	' failure in the game and it only happens when the crook is next to you,
2601               	; 	' which is exactly when you are not looking at the floor.
2602               	; 	'
2603               	; 	' Kelly (slot 0) + Harry (slot 1) + two obstacles = four. Provably never
2604               	; 	' dropped, on any band, in any situation.

2606               	; 	DIM obx(8)			' x within the screen
2607               	; 	DIM obd(8)			' 0 = moving left, 1 = right
2608               	; 	DIM obh(8)			' art-bottom height above the slab
2609               	; 	DIM obc(8)			' cell column, radios only -- they are chars
2610               	; 	DIM obp(8)			' bounce phase, balls only
2611               	; 	DIM obht(8)			' hit refractory, per obstacle -- see coll_obst
2612               	;
2613               	; 	DIM cok(4)			' this screen's collectible, per band
2614               	; 	DIM coc(4)			' its column
2615               	; 	DIM takn(4)			' 32 bits: which bands have been cleaned out

2617               	; 	' ---------------------------------------------------------------- state
2618               	; 	' Kelly
2619               	; 	' klv 0..3 (0 = floor 1, 3 = roof), klsc 0..7, klx 0..255
2620               	; 	' Harry the same. NOTHING in this program is a world coordinate.

2622               	; 	' EVERYTHING IS BUILT BEFORE THE TITLE IS DRAWN, NOT BEHIND IT.

2625               	; 	' is needed to put text on a screen: draw the title immediately, then

2629               	; 	'
2630               	; 	' IT MADE THE TITLE APPEAR SOONER AND ARRIVE DEAD. A third of a second of
2631               	; 	' a finished screen that was not yet reading the keyboard -- long enough to
2632               	; 	' swallow the first digit of 8-3-8, and reported as a start press that did

2636               	; 	' So the work moved back in front. The screen appears later and is live on

2916               	; setup_font:
2917               cvb_SETUP_FONT
2918               	; 	' Flicker stays OFF. CVBasic's is all-or-nothing -- it rotates all 32
2919               	; 	' slots, so Kelly would strobe too, and he is the one thing the player
2920               	; 	' must never lose. He is sprite 0 instead: the VDP drops the
2921               	; 	' HIGHEST-numbered sprites on an over-full scanline, so slot 0 is the
2922               	; 	' one slot that can never disappear.
2923               	; 	SPRITE FLICKER OFF
2924 ABA0 0200  20 	li r0,>0400
     ABA2 0400     
2925 ABA4 F800  30 	socb r0,@mode
     ABA6 834E     
2926               	;
2927               	; 	' THE ONE AND ONLY BANK SWITCH THE PROGRAM EVER MAKES, and it happens
2928               	; 	' here, before the first frame.
2929               	; 	'
2930               	; 	' There are two data banks now. Bank 1 holds everything read while the
2931               	; 	' game is running -- sprite and store art, the templates, the lookup
2932               	; 	' tables -- and it is selected at the end of this routine and never
2933               	; 	' changed again, so every VARPTR/PEEK read in the program is reading a
2934               	; 	' page that is permanently mapped. That is the property that makes
2935               	; 	' banking safe here: a missed BANK SELECT returns bytes from the wrong
2936               	; 	' page with no error at build or run time, so the safest number of
2937               	; 	' switches during play is none.
2938               	; 	'
2939               	; 	' Bank 2 exists to hold data that is read ONCE, at setup, and never
2940               	; 	' again. The font is exactly that: two DEFINEs copy it into VRAM and
2941               	; 	' nothing reads font_bits or font_col for the rest of the run. So it can
2942               	; 	' live on a page that is mapped for the length of those two statements.
2943               	; 	'
2944               	; 	' IF THIS EVER FAILS IT FAILS LOUDLY. Select the wrong bank here and the
2945               	; 	' font is garbage on the title screen, immediately and unmistakably --
2946               	; 	' which is the same diagnostic the font used to provide by staying out of
2947               	; 	' the banks altogether, recovered for free.
2948               	; 	#if TI994A
2949               	; 	BANK SELECT 2
2950 ABA8 04E0  34 	clr @>6008
     ABAA 6008     
2951               	; 	#endif
2952               	;
2953               	; 	DEFINE CHAR 32,59,font_bits
2954 ABAC 0204  20 	li r4,32
     ABAE 0020     
2955 ABB0 0205  20 	li r5,15104
     ABB2 3B00     
2956 ABB4 0200  20 	li r0,cvb_FONT_BITS
     ABB6 602A     
2957 ABB8 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     ABBA A980     
2958 ABBC A1FA     	data define_char
2959               	; 	' Without this the font keeps whatever CVBasic left in the colour table --
2960               	; 	' white on transparent -- which over a green store made the HUD unreadable.
2961               	; 	'
2962               	; 	' THIS WAS A VPOKE LOOP AND IT WAS THE SLOWEST THING IN THE BOOT: 1,416
2963               	; 	' writes of one constant, paced by 24 WAITs, which is what made the title
2964               	; 	' fill in visibly instead of appearing. DEFINE COLOR does the same job in a
2965               	; 	' single call with interrupts off, and it writes all three screen thirds
2966               	; 	' itself -- define_color always takes the LDIRVM3 triple-copy path, which is
2967               	; 	' also why esc_deck_col and floor0_colour below CANNOT use it: they patch
2968               	; 	' one third each.
2969               	; 	'
2970               	; 	' The table is 472 identical bytes (genfont.py emits it beside the glyphs).
2971               	; 	' It reads as waste and is not: it lives in the data bank, which had 860
2972               	; 	' bytes spare, while the loop it replaced cost time in the one place the
2973               	; 	' player is made to wait.
2974               	; 	DEFINE COLOR 32,59,font_col

     ABC0 0020

     ABC4 3B00

     ABC8 6202

     ABCC A980

2982               	; 	' FONT IS. Forty characters -- ten letters, four cells each -- drawn at
2983               	; 	' 16x16 so the game's name reads as a name rather than as a line of body
2984               	; 	' text. It is 640 bytes of pattern and colour and bank 1 had 370 free, so
2985               	; 	' it could not go there; it did not need to, because it is read ONCE, by
2986               	; 	' these two statements, and never again.
2987               	; 	'
2988               	; 	' Loading it inside the bank-2 window the font already opens means the
2989               	; 	' program still makes exactly ONE bank switch in its life.
2990               	; 	' IN TWO PIECES, AND THE SPLIT IS NOT TIDINESS. The character table has
2991               	; 	' 0..31, 91..95 and 182..207 free -- sixty-three codes, but the longest
2992               	; 	' run is thirty-two and the face needs forty. Loading it as one block at
2993               	; 	' 182 ran it into the RADAR CANVAS at 208, and S and T came out as the
2994               	; 	' scanner's green diagonals on a screen with no radar on it.
2995               	; 	'

3327               	;
3328               	; 	' THE JUMP ARC IS A TABLE, not integration. That makes the 14 px apex a
3329               	; 	' property of the data rather than of a fixed-point velocity that has to
3330               	; 	' be tuned, and it keeps every comparison in the jump 8-bit and unsigned.
3331               	; 	' DESIGN.md 5a depends on the apex being exactly 14.
3332               	; 	'
3333               	; 	' THIRTY FRAMES WITH NINE OF THEM AT THE APEX. The first version was 24
3334               	; 	' frames that touched 14 for only four, which made every jump a timing
3335               	; 	' test rather than a decision -- you had to leave the ground on exactly
3336               	; 	' the right frame or clip the thing you were jumping. Widening the
3337               	; 	' plateau rather than raising the apex keeps the ball arithmetic in
3338               	; 	' DESIGN.md 5a intact (the apex is what that depends on) while making the
3339               	; 	' window forgiving: the player still has to CHOOSE to jump, but no longer
3340               	; 	' has to be frame-perfect about it.
3341               	; 	' THE ARC IS A TABLE, not thirty assignments -- each of those compiled to
3342               	; 	' several bytes of code, and the fixed area is the binding budget.
3343               	; 	#jat = VARPTR jarc_tbl(0)

3397               	;
3398               	; 	' THE FONT'S COLOUR TABLE WAS 472 BYTES OF ONE REPEATED VALUE, which is a
3399               	; 	' fifth of what the fixed area had left. DEFINE COLOR copies such a table
3400               	; 	' out of ROM into all three screen thirds; writing the constant straight
3401               	; 	' into the colour table does the same job for the price of a loop, and
3402               	; 	' the loop runs once, at boot.
3403               	; 	'
3404               	; 	' The colour table is at >2000 and the VDP mirrors it once per screen
3405               	; 	' third, >800 apart. Both numbers were read out of the GENERATED assembly
3406               	; 	' -- define_color's `ai r0,>2000` and LDIRVM3's `ai r0,>0800` -- rather
3407               	; 	' than assumed, because a wrong base here would paint over the pattern
3408               	; 	' table and the failure would look like corrupt artwork.
3409               	; 	'
3410               	; 	' Paced: a few hundred VDP writes in one frame are silently dropped.
3411               	; 	' THE SCANNER'S COLOURS ARE THREE BLOCKS REPEATED SIXTEEN TIMES EACH, so
3412               	; 	' the table shipped 384 bytes to say 24 bytes' worth. Same trick as the
3413               	; 	' font: write the colour table directly. >2000 is the colour table's base
3414               	; 	' and >800 the stride between screen thirds -- the same layout DEFINE COLOR
3415               	; 	' walks for us in setup_font, which this cannot use because it is cheaper to
3416               	; 	' expand 24 bytes here than to ship 384 in the bank.
3417               	; 	' NOTHING IS UNDER THE GROUND FLOOR, SO NOTHING SHOULD BE GREEN THERE.
3418               	; 	' A floor bar is five pixels of yellow over three of the green air
3419               	; 	' belonging to the floor BELOW it (see SLAB), which is right for three of
3420               	; 	' the four bars and wrong for the last one: below floor 0 there is no
3421               	; 	' floor, only the scanner, and the green read as a strip of shop with
3422               	; 	' nothing in it.
3423               	; 	'
3424               	; 	' NO NEW CHARACTER IS NEEDED, BECAUSE THE COLOUR TABLE HAS THREE COPIES
3425               	; 	' -- one per eight screen rows -- and the bands land such that each bar
3426               	; 	' sits in a different third:
3427               	; 	'
3428               	; 	'     band 0 roof   rows  1-5    bar row  5   third 0
3429               	; 	'     band 1        rows  6-10   bar row 10   third 1
3430               	; 	'     band 2        rows 11-15   bar row 15   third 1
3431               	; 	'     band 3 GROUND rows 16-20   bar row 20   third 2
3432               	; 	'
3433               	; 	' so recolouring SLAB in third 2 alone reaches the ground floor's bar and
3434               	; 	' nothing else. The same third also holds the scanner, but the scanner
3435               	; 	' does not use these characters. This is the same mechanism that once hid
3436               	; 	' a bug for months (CLAUDE.md 3A, the blanked-in-one-third note) used
3437               	; 	' deliberately for once.
3438               	; 	'
3439               	; 	' Only the three bottom lines change, and only their BACKGROUND: SLAB has
3440               	; 	' no ink there and SLABE's brick keeps its grey.
3441               	; floor0_colour:
3442               cvb_FLOOR0_COLOUR
3443               	; 	' TWO CHARACTERS, THE SAME THREE SCAN LINES, ONE ROUTINE. Both blocks
3444               	; 	' were written out in full and differed only in which character and which
3445               	; 	' colour byte -- eleven statements twice, including the multiply-by-eight
3446               	; 	' done by doubling (`*` compiles to a real TMS9900 MPY, which clobbers r0,
3447               	; 	' CLAUDE.md 3A).
3448               	; 	f0c = CH_SLAB

3653               	; 	' ======================================================================
3654               	; 	' TITLE
3655               	; 	' ======================================================================
3656               	; 	' DRAWING THE TITLE AND WAITING ON IT ARE TWO ROUTINES, because the boot
3657               	; 	' does something between them: the rest of setup runs while this is on
3658               	; 	' screen. They used to be one, which is why the title could not be shown
3659               	; 	' until everything was ready.
3660               	; 	' THE TITLE IS A DISPLAY LIST IN A ROM BANK, not twelve PRINT ATs.
3661               	; 	'
3662               	; 	' CVBasic embeds a string literal in the FIXED AREA, which is the only
3663               	; 	' budget that cannot be grown -- linkticart writes exactly three loader
3664               	; 	' pages and discards the rest, and they are the 32K expansion's RAM at
3665               	; 	' >A000 rather than cart ROM. 190 characters of title text were sitting
3666               	; 	' in the scarcest place in the program.
3667               	; 	'
3668               	; 	' AND THE REAL POINT IS WHAT IT COSTS NEXT TIME. With the text in a
3669               	; 	' table, changing what the title says or where it sits is an edit to
3670               	; 	' assets/gentitle.py and a rebuild. It costs bank bytes, of which there
3671               	; 	' are thousands, instead of fixed-area bytes, of which there are tens.
3672               	; 	'
3673               	; 	' The table is `row, col, length, bytes...` with 255 to end. ROW AND
3674               	; 	' COLUMN rather than a 16-bit screen offset, because reassembling one
3675               	; 	' from two bytes needs a multiply, and on the TMS9900 MPY clobbers r0 --
3676               	; 	' the next line that reads the product's variable gets the HIGH word
3677               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A). Five doublings have no such hazard and are smaller.

3803               	;
3804               	; 	' NO ALPHA LOCK CALIBRATION, AND THERE USED TO BE ONE.
3805               	; 	'
3806               	; 	' The premise was that ALPHA LOCK shares a line with the joystick's
3807               	; 	' VERTICAL axis, so a latched key reports a direction that is never
3808               	; 	' released -- fatal here, where down is the duck and up is the lift. The
3809               	; 	' guard sampled the axis for forty frames before listening and then
3810               	; 	' ignored any direction that had been held for essentially all of them.
3811               	; 	'
3812               	; 	' IT WAS REMOVED BECAUSE THE PREMISE DOES NOT HOLD UP.
3813               	; 	'
3814               	; 	'   * CLAUDE.md claimed every other game here dodged the problem by not
3815               	; 	'     reading up/down. EIGHT of them do read it -- Adventire, Astiroids,
3816               	; 	'     HardHatMack, Ms. Pac-Man, RallyX, Structris, UFO, Bust-A-Bobble --
3817               	; 	'     and not one has a calibration or has ever shown the fault.
3818               	; 	'   * It never fired on the machine this is developed on: the notice it
3819               	; 	'     prints when it detects a stuck axis has never appeared.
3820               	; 	'   * The original evidence was that the game "came up and would not
3821               	; 	'     start" -- and the first version BLOCKED until the axis cleared. That
3822               	; 	'     symptom is indistinguishable from the several input bugs since found
3823               	; 	'     and fixed for real: keys arriving at a screen that was not listening
3824               	; 	'     yet. The diagnosis was probably one of those.
3825               	; 	'
3826               	; 	' It also cost two bugs of its own: forty frames of a drawn but deaf title
3827               	; 	' screen, which swallowed the first digit of 8-3-8, and a wrong theory
3828               	; 	' about keyboard noise that led to a filter which ate real presses.
3829               	; 	'
3830               	; 	' If a stuck axis ever does appear it will be obvious -- the player will
3831               	; 	' duck or ride the lift without asking -- and the guard is in the history.
3832               	;

3873               	; 	' THE MARQUEE CHASES WHILE THE TITLE WAITS.
3874               	; 	'
3875               	; 	' ONLY TWO CHARACTERS CHANGE PER STEP. At any moment exactly one of the
3876               	; 	' four lamps is blank; a step lights the one that was blank and blanks the
3877               	; 	' next one round. Redefining all four would be twice the work for the same
3878               	; 	' picture.
3879               	; 	'
3880               	; 	' IT IS BELOW THE INPUT READS, deliberately. This loop's history is input
3881               	; 	' bugs -- a screen that was drawn but not listening, a keypress eaten by a
3882               	; 	' stability filter -- so nothing that is merely decoration goes in front of
3883               	; 	' the polling. A dropped frame of animation is invisible; a dropped
3884               	; 	' keypress is what took three sessions to find.
3885               	; 	' `bphs` IS WHICH LAMP IS DARK, and a step is: light that one, move on,
3886               	; 	' darken the next. The character number is arithmetic rather than a
3887               	; 	' four-way branch -- DEFINE CHAR takes an expression, so the whole chase
3888               	; 	' is two calls and no `IF` ladder. The ladder version was eight DEFINE
3889               	; 	' CHARs across four branches and cost about three hundred bytes for the
3890               	; 	' same picture.
3891               	; 	'
3892               	; 	' TWO CALLS, NOT FIVE. Lighting all four and then darkening one is the
3893               	; 	' same result and reads more simply, but two separate DEFINEs can have a
3894               	; 	' vblank between them, so the sign would show ALL lamps lit for a frame
3895               	; 	' every step -- a flash rather than a chase. Only ever changing the two
3896               	; 	' lamps that actually change cannot do that.

4056               	;
4057               	; 	' 8-3-8 IS EDGE-TRIGGERED AND ANY STRAY DIGIT RESETS IT (see title_wait).
4058               	; 	'
4059               	; 	' It used to read cont1.key raw every pass and test only for the digit it
4060               	; 	' wanted next. That worked -- but only because 8-3-8 ALTERNATES, so holding
4061               	; 	' 8 cannot advance past the first step. It is an accident of the sequence
4062               	; 	' rather than a design, and it had two costs: 8,5,3,9,8 opened this page as
4063               	; 	' readily as 8,3,8, and a key that READS as held for many frames got a free
4064               	; 	' walk through the state machine.
4065               	; 	'
4066               	; 	' That second one is not hypothetical on this machine. ALPHA LOCK shorts a
4067               	; 	' keyboard line -- and Classic99 defaults to invertcaps, so it reads DOWN
4068               	; 	' with the host's Caps Lock UP -- and this page was reached twice from
4069               	; 	' single keypresses while testing an unrelated change.
4070               	; 	'
4071               	; 	' The reset is the DEFAULT rather than a test for a particular wrong digit:
4072               	; 	' Bust-A-Bobble resets only on a stray 3 and still lets 8,5,3,8 through.
4073               	; 	' ------------------------------------------------------- 838 setup page
4074               	; setup838:
4075               cvb_SETUP838
4076               	; 	CLS
4077 B376 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     B378 A980     
4078 B37A A0FC     	data cls
4079               	; 	' ONE PROMPT AT A TIME, NOTHING ELSE ON THE SCREEN, AND NO NUMBERS UNTIL
4080               	; 	' THEY ARE TYPED. There is no heading and no instructions: a page showing
4081               	; 	' exactly one question does not need to explain that one digit answers it,
4082               	; 	' and the second question does not exist until the first is answered.
4083               	; 	'
4084               	; 	' Showing the CURRENT values first was the obvious thing and it cost more
4085               	; 	' than it gave -- two draw routines, a "fire keeps what is shown" escape to
4086               	; 	' make the display mean something, and the defaults had to be applied here
4087               	; 	' as well as in new_game so the page had numbers to show at all. None of it
4088               	; 	' survives: every digit on screen is one the player just typed. Four
4089               	; 	' strings became two, a two-field loop became a straight line, and the page
4090               	; 	' got SMALLER while getting quieter.

4758               	;
4759               	; 	' ======================================================================
4760               	; 	' DRAWING THE STORE -- four blits, once per screen crossing
4761               	; 	' ======================================================================
4762               	; 	' This is the whole cost of the flip, and it is paid on a discrete event
4763               	; 	' rather than every frame. RallyX's pan repaints 576 chars every time the
4764               	; 	' camera moves one cell; this repaints 640 about once every two seconds
4765               	; 	' of running.
4766               	; 	' SPRITES OFF BEFORE THE BLIT, NOT AFTER IT. This routine WAITs between
4767               	; 	' bands -- one band a frame, because a burst of VDP writes past a few
4768               	; 	' dozen in one frame is silently dropped -- so painting the new screen
4769               	; 	' takes several frames, and for all of them the OLD screen's actors and
4770               	; 	' obstacles were still sitting on top of it. Following Harry through a
4771               	; 	' seam showed him and every cart from the floor he had just left,
4772               	; 	' standing on a shop that was assembling itself underneath them.
4773               	; 	'
4774               	; 	' They are put back by the normal draw on the same pass, so the crossing
4775               	; 	' reads as a cut rather than as a dissolve with ghosts in it.
4776               	; 	' EACH BAND IS FINISHED BEFORE THE FRAME IT IS DRAWN IN ENDS, and the
4777               	; 	' bands go TOP DOWN. Both halves of that matter.
4778               	; 	'
4779               	; 	' The blit paints the template -- shelves, pillars and all -- and the
4780               	; 	' radios and prizes then take out the fixtures they stand in. Those two
4781               	; 	' used to be four frames apart: all four bands blitted with a WAIT
4782               	; 	' between them, and only afterwards the clearing. So every screen change
4783               	; 	' showed its counters and beams for several frames and then erased them,
4784               	; 	' which reads as the shop flickering rather than as it being drawn.
4785               	; 	'
4786               	; 	' TOP DOWN because a band's beam tops are stamped into the SLAB ROW OF
4787               	; 	' THE BAND ABOVE. Going bottom-up, band 1's blit would paint over the
4788               	; 	' beam tops band 0 had just put there. Going top-down the band above is
4789               	; 	' always already drawn, so everything a band needs -- its own cells and
4790               	; 	' the row it borrows overhead -- is final by the time its WAIT arrives.
4791               	; 	'
4792               	; 	' `3 - dq` rather than `FOR dlv = 3 TO 0 STEP -1`: dlv is an unsigned
4793               	; 	' byte, so counting down past zero wraps to 255 and the loop never ends
4794               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A).
4795               	; draw_screen:

4906               	; 	' A SUPPORT BEAM HAS TO REACH THE FLOOR IT HOLDS UP, AND THAT FLOOR IS
4907               	; 	' NOT IN ITS OWN BAND. A beam fills its band's four air rows, so its top

4909               	; 	' five pixels of bar over three of green (see SLAB), so the beam stopped

4911               	; 	' misses the floor, which is exactly what it was.

5719               	; 			' THE BALL IS ON THE GROUND WHEN HE GETS TO IT.
5720               	; 			'
5721               	; 			' The bounce phase used to be `lx AND 31` -- a byte out of
5722               	; 			' the placement table, which is to say arbitrary. Run onto
5723               	; 			' a screen and the first ball might be at the bottom of its
5724               	; 			' arc, where a jump clears it, or at the top, where it has
5725               	; 			' to be ducked, and nothing on the way in told you which.
5726               	; 			' Sometimes you could keep running and jump it; sometimes
5727               	; 			' the same approach at the same speed could not be jumped
5728               	; 			' at all. That is not difficulty, it is a coin toss.
5729               	; 			'
5730               	; 			' So the phase is worked BACKWARDS from the meeting. He
5731               	; 			' closes 4 px a pass and the ball 2, so they meet in
5732               	; 			' (gap / 6) passes; the phase advances one a pass and wraps
5733               	; 			' at 32, so seeding it with the NEGATIVE of that lands it on
5734               	; 			' phase 0 -- the ground -- exactly as they arrive.
5735               	; 			'
5736               	; 			' The gap is the same either way round: he enters at one
5737               	; 			' wall and the ball starts `stag` in from the other, so it
5738               	; 			' is 232 - stag whichever direction the floor runs.
5739               	; 			'
5740               	; 			' It stays forgiving rather than exact. The arc is flat near
5741               	; 			' the bottom, so anything within eight passes either side is
5742               	; 			' still under the jump; and it only holds for an unbroken
5743               	; 			' run, which is the case the player is entitled to read off
5744               	; 			' the screen. Duck, stop or take a hit and everything after
5745               	; 			' is out of step again -- which is the game.
5746               	; 			obp(li) = lx AND 31
5747 BE86 D020  34 	movb @cvb_LX,r0
     BE88 21FD     
5748 BE8A 0201  20 	li r1,7936   ; 31*256
     BE8C 1F00     
5749 BE8E 0541  14 	inv r1

6615               	; 		' HE IS STANDING ON A STEP, so he moves at the STEP's rate: 2 px
6616               	; 		' across and 1 up PER PASS -- the staircase's own slope, and exactly
6617               	; 		' what one phase of esc_tick moves the pattern by.
6618               	; 		'
6619               	; 		' NOT `fdv`, WHICH IS THE WHOLE POINT. Everything else in this loop
6620               	; 		' is paced by the frame delta, and pacing him that way too made him
6621               	; 		' outrun the steps the moment a pass cost more than one frame: his
6622               	; 		' feet started planted on a tread and ended floating above it.
6623               	; 		' Pacing the ANIMATION by fdv instead is worse -- four phases cannot
6624               	; 		' be stepped by 2 or 3 without aliasing, and the staircase runs
6625               	; 		' backwards (see esc_tick). The only arrangement that cannot drift
6626               	; 		' is the one where both are driven by the same fixed step, so the
6627               	; 		' rider is clocked by the pass, like the steps he is standing on.
6628               	; 		'
6629               	; 		' THE FIRST FEW PASSES ARE THE STEP ON. Walking on, his feet are on
6630               	; 		' the floor and the bottom tread is 4 to 7 px above them, so he
6631               	; 		' climbs at 2 px a pass until he catches it (the tread is rising at
6632               	; 		' 1, so the gap closes at 1 a pass) and then rides with it. Jumping
6633               	; 		' on he lands ON a tread, so eson is 0 and this never runs.

7165               	; 		' THE FIRST STEP OFF THE MARK IS ALWAYS HEARD. sfw is a distance --
7166               	; 		' a step every fifteen pixels -- so a short tap of the stick moved
7167               	; 		' him a few pixels and made NO sound at all. That does not read as
7168               	; 		' a short step, it reads as the controls being ignored, and it is
7169               	; 		' worst exactly where a player taps rather than holds: lining up a
7170               	; 		' jump, or edging around a hazard.
7171               	; 		'
7172               	; 		' Priming the accumulator to the threshold makes the very next pass
7173               	; 		' fire. It does not cheat the RATE: the trigger subtracts fifteen
7174               	; 		' rather than zeroing, so the pixels actually travelled still carry
7175               	; 		' into the following step and a held run comes out at 6.9 a second
7176               	; 		' either way.

8092               	; 	' THE VICTROLA, AS CHARACTERS. It never moves, so a sprite spent a
8093               	; 	' scan-line slot on something that can be painted once when the screen is
8094               	; 	' drawn -- and at one 16x16 sprite it could only ever be one colour and
8095               	; 	' one size. Four cells is twice the area for no sprite at all.
8096               	; 	'
8097               	; 	' It stands ON the slab, so it fills the band's rows 2 and 3; row 4 is
8098               	; 	' the floor bar itself and draw_prizes uses row 3 for a collectible,
8099               	; 	' which is why the two never share a screen (genstore keeps prizes off
8100               	; 	' the screens that carry hazards).
8101               	; 	'
8102               	; 	' rdall = 1 paints all four cells, 0 repaints only the top-right one --
8103               	; 	' the pulse. Same address arithmetic either way, so the two cannot drift.
8104               	; 	' A BEAM TOP HANGS OUT OF THE FLOOR ABOVE, and the beam it belongs to has
8105               	; 	' just been taken away. `beam_tops` stamps SLABP -- the floor bar with the
8106               	; 	' support carried up through its lower three pixel rows -- into the slab
8107               	; 	' row above every pillar, and it runs BEFORE the radios and prizes are
8108               	; 	' placed. Clearing a pillar's own cells therefore left three grey pixels
8109               	; 	' dangling from the ceiling with nothing under them.
8110               	; 	'
8111               	; 	' TESTED, NOT ASSUMED: only SLABP is put back to SLAB. The row above the

8114               	; 	' A SHELF RUN IS FIVE CELLS WIDE and a radio covers two, so one standing
8115               	; 	' on a counter punched a hole through its middle and left the ends either
8116               	; 	' side -- the same incoherence the dangling pillar had, and worse, because

9037               	;
9038               	; 	' ONE STEP OF A FRACTIONAL SPEED, FOR WHOEVER IS MOVING.
9039               	; 	'
9040               	; 	' `pacc` in and out, `psp64` in (sixty-fourths of a pixel per FRAME),
9041               	; 	' `pspd` out (whole pixels this pass). CVBasic has no locals, so the caller
9042               	; 	' stages its own accumulator in and takes it back out; that costs four
9043               	; 	' statements against the fourteen this used to be, written out per actor.
9044               	; 	'
9045               	; 	' Harry had the only copy. Kelly, the hazards and the bounce phase all need
9046               	; 	' the same thing -- everything the round clock judges has to advance by
9047               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAMES, or the loop rate becomes a difficulty dial and where the
9048               	; 	' player stands decides the outcome (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
9049               	; 	'
9050               	; 	' TWO DRAINS CAP THE STEP AT 2 PER FRAME whatever psp64 says (CLAUDE.md
9051               	; 	' 3A: N drains cap the speed at N, and the surplus leaks into a byte that
9052               	; 	' wraps). Every caller is under that: Kelly 102/64 = 1.6, the fastest
9053               	; 	' hazard 76/64 = 1.2, Harry 57/64 = 0.9, the bounce phase 25/64 = 0.4.
9054               	; 	'
9055               	; 	' FIVE FRAMES, AND THREE WAS TOO FEW. At 2 px a frame five frames is 10 px,
9056               	; 	' and to skip a position window an actor must start outside it on one side
9057               	; 	' and land outside on the other, which needs 12. Three was the original bug
9058               	; 	' in miniature: the lift screen runs at almost exactly 20 passes a second,
9059               	; 	' which IS fdv = 3, so every hitch there lost a frame. The clamp exists for
9060               	; 	' a genuine stall and at five it only fires for one.
9061               	; pace_step:

9542               	;
9543               	; 	' THE SIXTEENTH-PIXEL ACCUMULATOR. hx is one unsigned byte per screen
9544               	; 	' (2), so there is nowhere to keep a fraction -- the fraction lives here
9545               	; 	' and is spent as whole pixels. THREE IFs, not a loop and not a divide:
9546               	; 	' `%` and `/` both compile to a real TMS9900 DIV (CLAUDE.md 3A) and this
9547               	; 	' runs every pass.
9548               	; 	'
9549               	; 	' THE NUMBER OF DRAINS IS A CEILING ON THE SPEED, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE
9550               	; 	' POINT OF THIS COMMENT. Each IF can spend one whole pixel, so N drains
9551               	; 	' cap hspd at N px per pass NO MATTER WHAT hsp64 SAYS. The invariant is:
9552               	; 	'
9553               	; 	'     hacc is under 16 on entry, and hsp64 is at most 48,
9554               	; 	'     so hacc is under 64 here and three drains always suffice.
9555               	; 	'
9556               	; 	' KEEP hsp64 <= 48. This was quarter-pixels with TWO drains and the same
9557               	; 	' invariant written the same way -- "hsp4 is at most 8, so it can never
9558               	; 	' need a third" -- and it was correct until somebody set hsp4 = 9 without
9559               	; 	' re-reading it. The crook then ran at a flat 2.0 px/pass while every
9560               	; 	' comment, the design table and assets/checkchase.py all said 2.25, and
9561               	; 	' the surplus quarter leaked into hacc and wrapped the byte every 256
9562               	; 	' passes. Nothing failed; he simply arrived two thirds of a screen short
9563               	; 	' of his own escape. checkchase.py now counts these IFs and refuses a
9564               	; 	' speed the drains cannot deliver.
9565               	; 	'
9566               	; 	' 7, NOT 6, AND THE REASON IS MEASURED. Tracked off the reference video
9567               	; 	' (DESIGN.md 4a), the 2600's Kelly covers 0.40 screen widths a second and
9568               	; 	' its Harry 0.193 -- a ratio of 2.07. At hsp4 = 6 ours was 2.67, and the
9569               	; 	' crook visibly strolled. 7 brings it to 2.29. 8 would match the original
9570               	; 	' exactly and cannot be used: Kelly's route here is 1.95x Harry's, so a
9571               	; 	' speed ratio of 2.0 leaves the on-foot chase 0.2 s of slack, which is no
9572               	; 	' chase at all. checkchase.py holds the line.
9573               	; 	' STILL RUNNING FROM THE STAIRS -- and this has to come BEFORE the move,
9574               	; 	' not after it. It sat below the two `IF hmv` blocks, where all it could
9575               	; 	' still reach was the animation counter: he faced the right way, played
9576               	; 	' the run cycle and did not travel a pixel. He stood at the foot of the
9577               	; 	' flight looking busy.
9578               	; 	'

9673               	;
9674               	; 	' HE WALKS BY REAL TIME, NOT BY LOOP PASS -- one accumulate-and-drain per
9675               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAME rather than per pass. Everything that moves here used to be
9676               	; 	' per pass while the CLOCK is paced by the frame delta, so a busy screen
9677               	; 	' slowed Harry in real seconds and the clock did not slow with him: the
9678               	; 	' same uninterrupted escape finished with nine timer units in hand from a
9679               	; 	' light screen and none at all from the lift screen, decided by where the
9680               	; 	' player happened to be standing. Now he covers the same ground per second
9681               	; 	' wherever anybody is (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
9682               	; 	'
9683               	; 	' A LOOP, NOT A MULTIPLY. `*` compiles to a real TMS9900 MPY, and reading a
9684               	; 	' 16-bit variable straight after one returns the product's HIGH word
9685               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A). fdv is 1..3 here, so this is at most three adds.
9686               	; 	'
9687               	; 	' SIXTY-FOURTHS, AND ONLY TWO DRAINS -- both fall out of accumulating per
9688               	; 	' FRAME instead of per pass. He covers under a pixel a frame, so two drains
9689               	; 	' are ample where the per-pass version needed three; and the finer unit is
9690               	; 	' what makes the speed tunable at all. In sixteenths one step was about six
9691               	; 	' SECONDS of his route, so nothing landed near the buzzer; in sixty-fourths
9692               	; 	' it is about one and a half. Keep hsp64 <= 128: hacc is under 64 on entry,
9693               	; 	' so 64 + 128 stays inside a byte and two drains always suffice.
9694               	; 	'
9695               	; 	' AND THE STEP IS CLAMPED TO THREE FRAMES' WORTH, WHICH IS NOT A DETAIL.
9696               	; 	' Two tests sample his position once a pass and neither interpolates:
9697               	; 	'
9698               	; 	'   ARRIVAL   `hdx < 6` around the escalator or the roof door -- an ELEVEN
9699               	; 	'             pixel window. A step over 10 px can jump clean across it and
9700               	; 	'             he never arrives at all.
9701               	; 	'   THE CATCH `hdd < CATCHR` is 12, a 23-wide band, and Kelly closes 4 of
9702               	; 	'             it himself -- so Harry over ~18 px could pass through the Kop
9703               	; 	'             between two passes without either sample being inside it.
9704               	; 	'
9705               	; 	' The clamp and the drains live in pace_step now, with the reasoning; the
9706               	; 	' numbers above are what sized them. Measured: TIME 02 on the lift screen
9707               	; 	' against TIME 04 on a light one when the clamp was 3, and 00 against 09
9708               	; 	' before any of this.
9709               	; 	'
9710               	; 	' The ESCALATOR RIDE is deliberately untouched: it returns above this,
9711               	; 	' clocked one step per pass to stay locked to the moving staircase. A rider
9712               	; 	' advanced by the frame delta either drifts off the treads or makes the
9713               	; 	' steps run backwards (CLAUDE.md 3A, DESIGN.md 0f). It is about 3% of his

9716               	; 	' `hanim` still advances by hspd and is still an ODOMETER -- pixels
